title: Question
body_md:
Does the bigraded BV algebra structure persist when the
Poisson structure is non-unimodular?
head: environment

label: mainthm1.1
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{mainthm1.1}
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite-dimensional bigraded vector
space over $k$, and let
$A=\mathcal{O}(\Sigma)$ be equipped with a Poisson
bivector $\pi$ of degree $(0,-2)$.
Let $\gamma$ be the standard mixed volume form on $A$.
If the modular derivation determined by $\gamma$ is diagonalizable over $k$,
then $\mathrm{HP}^{\bullet,\bullet}(A)$ admits a
canonical Batalin--Vilkovisky algebra structure whose operator
has cohomological degree $(0,-1)$ and generates
the induced Schouten--Nijenhuis bracket.
head: environment

label: mainthm
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{mainthm}
Let $A=(\mathcal{O}(k^{m||n}),\pi)$ be an
admissible quadratic Poisson algebra,
and let
$A^!=(\mathcal{O}(k^{n\wedge m}),\pi^!)$
be its Koszul dual Poisson algebra.
Equip $A$ and $A^!$ with the mixed volume forms
$$
\begin{aligned}
\gamma=dx_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dx_m
 \wedge y_1^*\wedge\cdots\wedge y_n^*,\quad
\gamma^!=\xi_1^*\wedge\cdots\wedge\xi_m^*
 \wedge d\eta_1\wedge\cdots\wedge d\eta_n.
\end{aligned}
$$
Assume that the modular derivation of $A$ determined by $\gamma$ is diagonalizable over $k$.
Then the Koszul correspondence induces an isomorphism
$$
    \mathrm{HP}^{\bullet,\bullet}(A)
    \xrightarrow{\;\sim\;}
    \mathrm{HP}^{\bullet,\bullet}(A^!)
$$
of Batalin--Vilkovisky algebras, with the BV operators
determined by $\gamma$ and $\gamma^!$.
head: environment

title: Example
body_md:
Let $k^{m||n}=\mathrm{Span}_k\{x_1,\cdots, x_m, y_1,\cdots, y_n\}$
with
$|x_i|=(0,0)$ and $|y_j|=(1,0)$.
The coordinate degrees thus give the relations
$$
x_i x_a=x_a x_i,\qquad
x_i y_j=y_j x_i,\qquad
y_j y_b=-y_b y_j.
$$
Thus, as an ordinary associative algebra,
$\mathcal O(k^{m||n})=k[x_1,\ldots,x_m]\otimes
\Lambda(y_1,\ldots,y_n)$.

For the second space, let $k^{n\wedge m}=\mathrm{Span}_k\{\xi_1,\cdots,\xi_m,\eta_1,\cdots,\eta_n\}$, with $|\xi_i|=(0,-1)$ and $|\eta_j|=(-1,-1)$.
The commutation relations are
$$
\xi_i\xi_a=-\xi_a\xi_i,\qquad
\xi_i\eta_j=-\eta_j\xi_i,\qquad
\eta_j\eta_b=\eta_b\eta_j.
$$
With these degrees, both function algebras are bigraded commutative and form a Koszul dual pair \cite[Theorem~2.6]{CY}.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md: Let $A$ be a bigraded commutative algebra. A bivector field $\pi$ satisfying $[\pi,\pi]=0$ defines a \textit{Poisson algebra} $(A,\pi)$.
head: environment
name: Bigraded Poisson algebra

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $A$ be a bigraded algebra. A \textit{derivation} of $A$ with values in an $A$-module $M$ is a $k$-linear map $\upsilon: A \to M$ satisfying
$$
\upsilon(ab) = \upsilon(a)b + (-1)^{p(a)p(\upsilon)+w(a)w(\upsilon)}a\upsilon(b) \quad \text{for all homogeneous } a,b \in A,
$$
and $\upsilon(c)=0$ for every $c \in k$. 
We denote the set of such derivations by $\overline{\mathfrak X}(A,M)$, abbreviated to $\overline{\mathfrak X}(A)$ or $\operatorname{Der}(A)$ when $M=A$.
head: environment
name: Derivation

title: Definition
body_md:
Suppose $A$ is a bigraded Poisson algebra. A \textit{Poisson derivation} of $A$ is a derivation $\upsilon \in \mathrm{Der}(A)$ satisfying $$\upsilon (\{f,g\})=\{\upsilon (f),g\}+(-1)^{p(f)p(\upsilon)+w(f)w(\upsilon)}\{f,\upsilon (g)\}$$
    for any homogeneous elements $f,g\in A$.
head: environment
name: Poisson derivation

title: Definition
body_md:
Suppose $A$ is a bigraded commutative algebra.
For $p\ge 0$, the $A$-module of
$p$-th polyvectors, denoted by 
$\mathfrak{X}^p(A)$, is defined as the 
$p$-th bigraded symmetric product of
$
\mathfrak{X}^1(A)
$; that is,
$$
\mathfrak{X}^p(A):=\mathrm{Sym}^p_A(\mathfrak{X}^1(A)).
$$
The $A$-module of all polyvectors on $A$ is then
$$\mathfrak{X}^\bullet(A):=
\bigoplus_{p\ge 0}\mathfrak{X}^p(A).$$
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Following \cite[Definition~4.3]{CY}, let
$A=\mathcal{O}(\Sigma)$ be a bigraded Poisson algebra with
$\deg(\pi)=(0,-2)$.
Its Poisson cochain complex is defined by
$$
\mathrm{CP}^{s,t}(A)
=
\{P\in\mathfrak{X}^{\bullet}(A)
\mid \deg(P)=(-s,-t)\},
\qquad
\delta^\pi=[-,\pi]:
\mathrm{CP}^{s,t}(A)\longrightarrow
\mathrm{CP}^{s,t+1}(A).
$$
Its cohomology is denoted by $\mathrm{HP}^{s,t}(A)$.
head: environment
name: Poisson cochain complex

title: Definition
head: environment
name: Mixed differential forms

title: Definition
body_md:
The space of \textit{mixed vector fields} on $A$ is the subspace $$\tilde{\mathfrak{X}}^1(A):
=\Big\{\sum_{i=1}^{m}g_i\partial_{i}+\sum_{j=m+1}^{l}g_jz_j\mid g_i,g_j\in 
\tilde{\Omega}^0(A)\Big\}\subset\mathfrak X^\bullet(A).$$
For each integer $p\ge 1$, the space of \textit{mixed $p$-vector fields} is
$$
\tilde{\mathfrak X}^p(A):=\operatorname{Sym}_{\tilde\Omega^0(A)}^p(\tilde{\mathfrak X}^1(A))\subset\mathfrak X^\bullet(A),
$$
where the symmetric power is bigraded.
head: environment
name: Mixed vector fields

title: Definition
body_md: For a homogeneous mixed vector field $X$, the \textit{mixed contraction} $\tilde\iota_X$ is the derivation of bidegree $|X|$ on $\widetilde\Omega^\bullet(A)$ determined by $\tilde\iota_X(f)=0$ for $f\in\widetilde\Omega^0(A)$ and $\tilde\iota_X(\omega)=\langle\omega,X\rangle$ for $\omega\in\widetilde\Omega^1(A)$. It lowers mixed form length by one.
head: environment
name: Mixed contraction

label: mixedcartan
title: Proposition
head: environment
name: Mixed Cartan formula

title: Definition
body_md:
Following \cite[Definition~4.5]{CY}, let
$A=\mathcal{O}(\Sigma)$ be a bigraded Poisson algebra with
$\deg(\pi)=(0,-2)$.
Its mixed Poisson chain complex is defined by
$$
\widetilde{\mathrm{CP}}_{s,t}(A)
=
\widetilde{\Omega}^{s,t}(A),
\qquad
\partial_\pi=[\tilde{\iota}_\pi,\tilde d]:
\widetilde{\mathrm{CP}}_{s,t}(A)\longrightarrow
\widetilde{\mathrm{CP}}_{s,t-1}(A).
$$
Its homology is denoted by
$\widetilde{\mathrm{HP}}_{s,t}(A)$.
head: environment
name: Mixed Poisson chain complex

title: Definition
body_md:
A derivation $\upsilon\in \text{Der}(A)$ of an algebra $ A $ over $ k $ is called \textit{diagonalizable} (or \textit{semisimple}) if $A$ admits a decomposition of $ k $-vector spaces
$$
A = \bigoplus_{\lambda \in S} A_\lambda, \quad A_\lambda := \{a \in A \mid \upsilon (a) = \lambda a\},
$$ for some subset $ S \subseteq k $.
head: environment
name: Diagonalizable derivation

label: prop:canonical-volume
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:canonical-volume}
For every finite-dimensional bigraded space $\Sigma$, the form
$$
\gamma_{\mathrm{std}}=dz_1\wedge\cdots\wedge dz_m
\wedge z_{m+1}^*\wedge\cdots\wedge z_l^*
$$
is a mixed volume form. Every mixed volume form is a
nonzero scalar multiple of it, and is $\tilde d$-closed.
head: environment

label: lem:modular-poisson
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:modular-poisson}
Let $\gamma$ be a closed mixed volume form and let
$\upsilon=-\mathrm{Div}_\gamma(\pi)$.
Then $[\pi,\upsilon]=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\tilde d\gamma=0$,
$\partial_\pi\gamma=-\tilde dD_\gamma(\pi)
=\tilde\iota_\upsilon\gamma$.
The operators $\partial_\pi$ and $\tilde\iota_\upsilon$
both have degree $(0,-1)$, so the mixed Cartan formula gives
$$
D_\gamma([\pi,\upsilon])
=[\partial_\pi,\tilde\iota_\upsilon]\gamma
=\partial_\pi^2\gamma+\tilde\iota_\upsilon^2\gamma=0.
$$
Here $\tilde\iota_\upsilon^2=\tilde\iota_{\upsilon\wedge\upsilon}=0$,
since $|\upsilon|=(0,-1)$ and $\operatorname{char}k=0$.
Injectivity of $D_\gamma$ proves the assertion.
head: environment

label: prop2.14
title: Proposition
head: environment

label: cartan
title: Proof
body_md:
By the mixed Cartan formula \eqref{mixedcartanformula}, 
    \begin{align}\label{cartan}
\tilde{\iota}_{[P,\pi]}(\gamma)
=
(-1)^{w(P)}
\partial_\pi(\tilde{\iota}_P\gamma)
-
\tilde{\iota}_P(\partial_\pi\gamma).
\end{align}
Since $\tilde d\gamma=0$, we have $\partial_\pi\gamma=\tilde\iota_\upsilon\gamma$. Bigraded commutativity of contractions then gives
$$
\tilde\iota_\upsilon\tilde\iota_P\gamma
=(-1)^{|P||\upsilon|}\tilde\iota_P\tilde\iota_\upsilon\gamma
=(-1)^{w(P)}\tilde\iota_P(\partial_\pi\gamma).
$$
    The result follows by substitution into \eqref{cartan}.
head: environment

label: horiso
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\gamma$ is a mixed volume form, the map
$$
D_\gamma:
\mathrm{CP}^{s,t}(A)
\longrightarrow
\widetilde{\mathrm{CP}}_{u-s,v-t}(A;\upsilon),
\qquad
D_\gamma(P)=\tilde\iota_P\gamma,
$$
is an isomorphism of vector spaces.
By Proposition~\ref{prop2.14},
$$
\partial_\upsilon D_\gamma(P)
=(-1)^tD_\gamma(\delta^\pi P),
\qquad P\in\mathrm{CP}^{s,t}(A),
$$
because $w(P)=-t$.
Thus $D_\gamma$ identifies cycles and boundaries
in the two complexes.

More precisely, define
$$
F(P)=(-1)^{t(t-1)/2}D_\gamma(P),
\qquad P\in\mathrm{CP}^{s,t}(A).
$$
Since $\delta^\pi P\in\mathrm{CP}^{s,t+1}(A)$, we obtain
$$
F(\delta^\pi P)
=(-1)^{t(t+1)/2}D_\gamma(\delta^\pi P)
=\partial_\upsilon F(P).
$$
Hence $F$ is an isomorphism of complexes after reindexing
the target by $(s,t)\mapsto(u-s,v-t)$.
The asserted isomorphism follows.
head: environment

label: homotopy
title: Lemma
body_md:
The operators $\partial_\upsilon$ and $\tilde d$ satisfy
\begin{equation}\label{homotopy}
\partial_\upsilon\tilde d+\tilde d\partial_\upsilon
=-L_\upsilon.
\end{equation}
Moreover, $L_\upsilon$ commutes with both
$\partial_\upsilon$ and $\tilde d$, and
$L_\upsilon\gamma=0$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Using
$\partial_\pi\tilde d+\tilde d\partial_\pi=0$, we have
$$
\partial_\upsilon\tilde d+\tilde d\partial_\upsilon
=
-\bigl(\tilde\iota_\upsilon\tilde d
+\tilde d\tilde\iota_\upsilon\bigr)
=-L_\upsilon.
$$
Since $\partial_\upsilon^2=\tilde d^2=0$,
equation~\eqref{homotopy} implies
$[L_\upsilon,\partial_\upsilon]=[L_\upsilon,\tilde d]=0$.
Proposition~\ref{prop2.14}, applied to $P=1$, gives
$\partial_\upsilon\gamma=0$.
Together with $\tilde d\gamma=0$, this yields
$L_\upsilon\gamma=0$.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
With the notation above, 
for $\lambda\in k$, set
\begin{align*}
\mathrm{CP}^{s,t}_\lambda(A)
&:=
\{P\in\mathrm{CP}^{s,t}(A)
\mid[\upsilon,P]=\lambda P\},\\
\widetilde{\mathrm{CP}}^\lambda_{s,t}(A;\upsilon)
&:=
\{\alpha\in\widetilde{\mathrm{CP}}_{s,t}(A;\upsilon)
\mid L_\upsilon\alpha=\lambda\alpha\}.
\end{align*}
head: environment

label: diagonalizable
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{diagonalizable}
Suppose that $\overline{\upsilon}$ is diagonalizable
on $A$ over $k$.
Then the inclusions of the zero-eigenvalue subcomplexes
are homotopy equivalences. In particular,
$$
\widetilde{\mathrm{HP}}_{\bullet,\bullet}(A;\upsilon)
\cong
\mathrm{H}_{\bullet,\bullet}
\bigl(\widetilde{\mathrm{CP}}^0_{\bullet,\bullet}
(A;\upsilon)\bigr),\quad
\mathrm{HP}^{\bullet,\bullet}(A)
\cong
\mathrm{H}^{\bullet,\bullet}
\bigl(\mathrm{CP}^{\bullet,\bullet}_0(A)\bigr).
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
To obtain the eigenspace decompositions, take the eigencomponents of a finite homogeneous generating set of $A$. Their span $W\subset A$ is a finite-dimensional homogeneous $\overline\upsilon$-invariant subspace, because $\overline\upsilon$ is diagonalizable and preserves the bigrading. The subspace $W$ still generates $A$.

Restriction to $W$ gives an injective equivariant map
$$
\operatorname{Der}_k(A)
\longrightarrow
\operatorname{Hom}_k(W,A),
\qquad
D\longmapsto D|_W,
$$
where the action on the target is
$T\mapsto\overline\upsilon\circ T
-T\circ\overline\upsilon|_W$.
Choose an eigenbasis $e_1,\ldots,e_N$ of $W$, with $\overline\upsilon(e_i)=\lambda_i e_i$. Evaluation on this basis identifies the action on $\operatorname{Hom}_k(W,A)$ with $\bigoplus_{i=1}^N(\overline\upsilon-\lambda_i)$ on $A^{\oplus N}$, which is diagonalizable.

Every invariant subspace of a diagonalizable operator
is a direct sum of eigenspaces: the finitely many
eigencomponents of any vector are recovered by
polynomial spectral projections. The same argument
applies to invariant quotients. Consequently,
$[\overline\upsilon,-]$ is diagonalizable on
$\operatorname{Der}_k(A)$, and the shifted action
$[\upsilon,-]$ is diagonalizable on $\mathfrak X^1(A)$.
Since this action is a derivation of the wedge product,
tensor products and invariant quotients give
diagonalizability on
$\mathfrak X^r(A)=\operatorname{Sym}_A^r\mathfrak X^1(A)$
for every $r\geq1$. Together with the hypothesis on
$\mathfrak X^0(A)=A$, this yields
$$
\mathrm{CP}^{s,t}(A)
=
\bigoplus_{\lambda\in k}\mathrm{CP}^{s,t}_\lambda(A).
$$
Transporting this decomposition along the
eigenvalue-preserving isomorphism $D_\gamma$, we obtain
$$
\widetilde{\mathrm{CP}}_{s,t}(A;\upsilon)
=
\bigoplus_{\lambda\in k}
\widetilde{\mathrm{CP}}^\lambda_{s,t}(A;\upsilon).
$$
Both decompositions are algebraic direct sums.

Let $\iota_0$ and $p_0$ denote the inclusion of the
zero-eigenvalue chain subcomplex and the projection
onto it. By \eqref{homotopy},
\begin{equation}\label{homotopyid}
\left.
(\partial_\upsilon\tilde d+\tilde d\partial_\upsilon)
\right|_{\widetilde{\mathrm{CP}}^\lambda_{\bullet,\bullet}
(A;\upsilon)}
=
-\lambda\,\mathrm{id}.
\end{equation}
Define an operator $h$ of homological degree $(0,1)$ by
$$
h\big|_{\widetilde{\mathrm{CP}}^\lambda_{\bullet,\bullet}
(A;\upsilon)}
=
\begin{cases}
-\lambda^{-1}\tilde d,&\lambda\neq0,\\
0,&\lambda=0.
\end{cases}
$$
This operator is well defined because $\tilde d$
preserves eigenspaces and every element has only finitely many nonzero eigencomponents.
Equation~\eqref{homotopyid} gives
$$
\partial_\upsilon h+h\partial_\upsilon
=
\mathrm{id}-\iota_0p_0,
\qquad
p_0\iota_0=\mathrm{id}.
$$
Thus $\iota_0$ is a homotopy equivalence.

For cochains, let $F$ denote the isomorphism of complexes
constructed in Theorem~\ref{horiso}, and let $i_0$ and $q_0$ denote
the zero-eigenvalue inclusion and projection.
Then $H=F^{-1}hF$ has cohomological degree $(0,-1)$
and satisfies
$$
\delta^\pi H+H\delta^\pi
=
F^{-1}(\mathrm{id}-\iota_0p_0)F
=
\mathrm{id}-i_0q_0,
\qquad
q_0i_0=\mathrm{id}.
$$
Hence $i_0$ is also a homotopy equivalence.
The asserted homology and cohomology isomorphisms follow.
head: environment

label: diffcalculus
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{diffcalculus}
Let $\mathrm{H}^{\bullet,\bullet}$ and $\mathrm{H}_{\bullet,\bullet}$ 
be bigraded vector spaces.
A \textit{differential calculus} is a sextuple
$$
(\mathrm{H}^{\bullet,\bullet},
\mathrm{H}_{\bullet,\bullet}, \cup, \iota, [-,-], d)
$$
satisfying the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(1)] $(\mathrm{H}^{\bullet,\bullet},\cup,[-,-])$ is a 
bigraded Gerstenhaber
algebra.
\begin{itemize}
\item $(\mathrm{H}^{\bullet,\bullet},\cup)$ is a bigraded commutative algebra;
\item $(\mathrm{H}^{\bullet,\bullet},[-,-])$ is a Lie algebra of cohomological degree $(0,-1)$,
corresponding to actual bracket degree $(0,1)$ on polyvectors;
\item the bracket satisfies the bigraded Leibniz rule
$$
[P,Q\cup R]
=[P,Q]\cup R
+(-1)^{|P||Q|+w(Q)}\,Q\cup[P,R],
$$
for homogeneous elements $P, Q, R$;
\end{itemize}


\item[(2)] $\mathrm{H}_{\bullet,\bullet}$ is a bigraded (left) 
module over 
$(\mathrm{H}^{\bullet,\bullet}, \cup)$ via the map
$$
\iota: \mathrm{H}^{i,j}\otimes\mathrm{H}_{s,t}\to 
\mathrm{H}_{s-i,t-j},\;f\otimes p\mapsto \iota_fp,
$$
for any $f\in \mathrm{H}^{i,j}$ and $p \in \mathrm{H}_{s,t}$;
                
\item[(3)] There is a map $d: \mathrm{H}_{\bullet,\bullet}\to \mathrm{H}_{\bullet,\bullet+1}$ 
satisfying $d^2=0$.
With $L_f:=[\iota_f,d]=\iota_fd-(-1)^{w(f)}d\iota_f$, the Cartan identity for homogeneous $f,g\in\mathrm H^{\bullet,\bullet}$ is
\begin{align}\label{calculusformula}
\iota_{[f,g]}=[L_f,\iota_g] :={L}_{f}\iota_g-(-1)^{p(g)p(f)
+w(g)(w(f)+1)}\iota_g {L}_f.
\end{align}       
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Differential calculus

title: Example
body_md:
For a finite-dimensional bigraded space $\Sigma$ over $k$
and a Poisson bivector $\pi$ of degree $(0,-2)$ on
$A=\mathcal O(\Sigma)$, the sextuple
$$
(\mathrm{HP}^{\bullet,\bullet}(A),
\widetilde{\mathrm{HP}}_{\bullet,\bullet}(A),
\wedge,\tilde\iota,[-,-],\tilde d)
$$
is a differential calculus by \cite[Theorem~4.6]{CY}.
In particular, this applies to both members of the
admissible quadratic Koszul pair.
head: environment

label: diff calculus
title: Definition
head: environment
name: differential calculus with duality

label: diffcaldual
title: Corollary
body_md:
\label{diffcaldual}
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite-dimensional bigraded vector space
over a field $k$ of characteristic zero, and let
$A=\mathcal{O}(\Sigma)$ be equipped with a Poisson structure
$\pi$ of degree $(0,-2)$.
Let $\gamma\in\widetilde{\Omega}^{u,v}(A)$ be the
standard mixed volume form.
Assume that the derivation of $A$ corresponding to the modular vector field $\upsilon$ is diagonalizable over $k$.
Then
$$
\bigl(
\mathrm{HP}^{\bullet,\bullet}(A),
\widetilde{\mathrm{HP}}_{\bullet,\bullet}(A;\upsilon),
\wedge,\tilde\iota,[-,-],\tilde d
\bigr)
$$
is a differential calculus with duality,
with fundamental class $[\gamma]$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The mixed Cartan identity and the graded commutativity
of contractions give, for every homogeneous polyvector $P$,
$$
[\partial_\upsilon,\tilde\iota_P]
=
\tilde\iota_{[\pi,P]}
=
(-1)^{w(P)}\tilde\iota_{\delta^\pi P}.
$$
Hence contraction by a Poisson cocycle preserves twisted
cycles and boundaries, while contraction by a Poisson
coboundary induces the zero map on twisted homology.

Moreover,
$[L_\upsilon,\tilde\iota_P]
=
\tilde\iota_{[\upsilon,P]}$.
Thus contraction by a zero-eigenvalue cochain preserves
the zero-eigenvalue chain complex. Since
$[\upsilon,-]$ is a derivation of both the wedge product
and the Schouten bracket, these operations also preserve
the zero-eigenvalue cochain complex.

On the zero-eigenvalue chain complex,
$\partial_\upsilon\tilde d+\tilde d\partial_\upsilon=0$.
The mixed Cartan identity therefore descends to homology,
giving a differential calculus. By
Theorem~\ref{diagonalizable}, the zero-eigenvalue inclusions
identify this calculus with the asserted one, where
$\tilde d$ denotes the transported operator $B$.


Finally, $\partial_\upsilon\gamma=\tilde d\gamma=0$, and contraction with $[\gamma]$ gives the duality isomorphism of Theorem~\ref{horiso}.
head: environment

title: Definition
head: environment
name: Batalin--Vilkovisky algebra

label: thm:bv-duality
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{thm:bv-duality}
Let
$(\mathrm H^{\bullet,\bullet},\mathrm H_{\bullet,\bullet},
\cup,\iota,[-,-],d,\gamma)$
be a differential calculus with duality, and write
$\mathrm{PD}(a)=\iota_a\gamma$. Then
$\Delta=-\mathrm{PD}^{-1}\circ d\circ\mathrm{PD}$
has degree $(0,-1)$ and defines a Batalin--Vilkovisky
algebra structure on $\mathrm H^{\bullet,\bullet}$. For homogeneous
$a,b\in \mathrm H^{\bullet,\bullet}$, it satisfies
$$
[a,b]
=(-1)^{w(a)}
\bigl(\Delta(a\cup b)-\Delta(a)\cup b\bigr)
-a\cup\Delta(b).
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The degree of $\Delta$ is $(0,-1)$, since $\mathrm{PD}:\mathrm H^{s,t}\to\mathrm H_{u-s,v-t}$ and $d:\mathrm H_{s,t}\to\mathrm H_{s,t+1}$.
Moreover, $d^2=0$ and $d\gamma=0$ imply
$\Delta^2=0$ and $\Delta(1)=0$.

Applying the Cartan identity
$\iota_{[a,b]}=[[\iota_a,d],\iota_b]$ to $\gamma$,
and using $d\gamma=0$,
$\iota_{a\cup b}=\iota_a\iota_b$ and
$\mathrm{PD}^{-1}(\iota_a\omega)
=a\cup\mathrm{PD}^{-1}(\omega)$, we obtain
\begin{align}\label{eq:second-order}
   [a,b]
=(-1)^{w(a)}
\bigl(\Delta(a\cup b)-\Delta(a)\cup b\bigr)
-a\cup\Delta(b). 
\end{align}
The Leibniz rule for $[a,-]$, applied to \eqref{eq:second-order}, gives the second-order identity for $\Delta$; compare \cite[Proposition~1.2]{getzler1994batalin}. Together with $\Delta^2=0$, this makes $\Delta$ a BV operator.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Apply Theorem~\ref{thm:bv-duality} to the calculus with
duality in Corollary~\ref{diffcaldual}, using the operator
$B$ obtained from the zero-eigenvalue complex.
By Proposition~\ref{prop:canonical-volume}, any other mixed volume form
is $c\gamma$ with $c\in k^\times$. This leaves the modular
vector field, its eigenspaces and $B$ unchanged, and
replaces $\mathrm{PD}$ by $c\mathrm{PD}$. Hence
$\Delta=-\mathrm{PD}^{-1}B\mathrm{PD}$ is unchanged.
head: environment

label: rem:modular-class-bv
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:modular-class-bv}
For a Poisson cocycle $P$ in the zero eigenspace,
$\Delta[P]=[-\mathrm{Div}_\gamma(P)]$.
In particular,
$
\Delta[\pi]=[\upsilon].
$
Indeed, $[\pi,\pi]=0$ and Lemma~\ref{lem:modular-poisson} show that $\pi$ is a Poisson cocycle in the zero eigenspace. Substituting $\upsilon=-\mathrm{Div}_\gamma(\pi)$ gives the formula.
head: environment

title: Definition
body_md:
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite-dimensional bigraded vector space,
and let $A=\mathcal{O}(\Sigma)=\operatorname{Sym}_k(\Sigma^*)$.
A Poisson structure $\pi$ on $A$ is called \emph{quadratic}
if its coefficients are homogeneous polynomials of degree two.
Equivalently, in homogeneous linear coordinates
$z_1,\ldots,z_l$, it has the form
$$
\pi=\sum_{a,b,c,d=1}^{l}
C^{a,b}_{c,d}\,z_a z_b\,
\partial_{z_c}\wedge\partial_{z_d},
\qquad C^{a,b}_{c,d}\in k.
$$
Here polynomial degree refers to the symmetric-algebra grading,
independently of the bigrading. Following \cite{CY}, a
quadratic Poisson structure of degree $(0,-2)$ is
called \emph{admissible quadratic}.
head: environment
name: Quadratic Poisson structure

label: def:diagonalPoisson
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:diagonalPoisson}
Let $\Sigma$ be a finite-dimensional bigraded vector space,
and let $A=\mathcal{O}(\Sigma)$.
A Poisson structure $\pi$ on $A$ is called \emph{diagonal}
if there exist homogeneous linear coordinates
$z_1,\ldots,z_l$ such that
$$
\pi=\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq l}
c_{ij}z_i z_j\,
\partial_{z_i}\wedge\partial_{z_j},
\qquad c_{ij}\in k.
$$
In this case, $\pi$ is said to be diagonal with respect
to these coordinates.
head: environment
name: Diagonal Poisson structure

label: quadratic poisson Koszul
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{quadratic poisson Koszul}
Let $\pi$ and $\pi^!$ be the quadratic bivectors on $k^{m||n}$ and $k^{n\wedge m}$ related by \eqref{corres}. Then $\pi$ is Poisson if and only if $\pi^!$ is Poisson.
head: environment
name: Chen--Yu

label: prop:diagonal-koszul
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
The first expression follows from
Definition~\ref{def:diagonalPoisson}, with the coordinates
ordered as $x_1,\ldots,x_m,y_1,\ldots,y_n$.
Let $E_i=x_i\frac{\partial}{\partial x_i}$ and $F_s=y_s\frac{\partial}{\partial y_s}$ be the coordinate Euler derivations, each of bidegree $(0,0)$. They commute pairwise, and \eqref{eq:diagonal-original} is a constant linear combination of their pairwise polyvector products. The Schouten Leibniz rule therefore gives $[\pi,\pi]=0$.

Let $\Psi$ denote the polyvector correspondence
\eqref{corres}.
Reordering its images according to the bigraded sign rule gives
$\Psi\bigl(x_i x_j\,
\partial_{x_i}\wedge\partial_{x_j}\bigr)
=\xi_i\xi_j\,
\partial_{\xi_i}\wedge\partial_{\xi_j}$, 
$\Psi\bigl(y_s y_t\,
\partial_{y_s}\wedge\partial_{y_t}\bigr)
=\eta_s\eta_t\,
\partial_{\eta_s}\wedge\partial_{\eta_t}$ and 
$\Psi\bigl(x_i y_s\,
\partial_{x_i}\wedge\partial_{y_s}\bigr)
=-\xi_i\eta_s\,
\partial_{\xi_i}\wedge\partial_{\eta_s}.$
This proves \eqref{eq:diagonal-dual}.
Theorem~\ref{quadratic poisson Koszul} implies that
$\pi^!$ is Poisson.
Finally, the coefficient transformation $(a_{ij},b_{st},c_{is})\mapsto(a_{ij},b_{st},-c_{is})$ is invertible, so every structure diagonal in the specified dual coordinates arises in this way.
head: environment

label: modulardual
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{modulardual}
Let $A=\mathcal O(k^{m||n})$ and
$A^!=\mathcal O(k^{n\wedge m})$ be equipped with
Koszul-dual quadratic Poisson structures $\pi$ and $\pi^!$
of degree $(0,-2)$, respectively.
Let $\upsilon$ and $\upsilon^!$ be their modular vector
fields with respect to the mixed volume forms
$\gamma$ and $\gamma^!$ chosen above.
Then the correspondence \eqref{corres} sends
$\upsilon$ to $\upsilon^!$.
Moreover, the derivation of $A$ corresponding to $\upsilon$ is diagonalizable over $k$ if and only if the derivation of $A^!$ corresponding to $\upsilon^!$ is.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Let $\Psi$ denote the isomorphism of polyvector algebras
given by \eqref{corres}, and let $\Phi$ be the corresponding
isomorphism of mixed differential forms, determined by
$$x_i\longmapsto\partial_{\xi_i},\quad
dx_i\longmapsto\xi_i^*,\quad
\partial_{y_j}\longmapsto\eta_j,\quad
y_j^*\longmapsto d\eta_j.$$
By \cite[Proposition~3.19]{CY}, these maps satisfy
$\Phi\tilde d=\tilde d\Phi$ and $
\Phi\tilde\iota_P=\tilde\iota_{\Psi(P)}\Phi.$
Moreover, the chosen volume forms satisfy
$\Phi(\gamma)=\gamma^!$.
Writing $D_\gamma(P)=\tilde\iota_P\gamma$ and
$D_{\gamma^!}(Q)=\tilde\iota_Q\gamma^!$, we therefore obtain
$\Phi D_\gamma=D_{\gamma^!}\Psi$.
It follows that
$$\Psi\mathrm{Div}_{\gamma}
=\Psi D_\gamma^{-1}\tilde dD_\gamma
=D_{\gamma^!}^{-1}\Phi\tilde dD_\gamma
=D_{\gamma^!}^{-1}\tilde dD_{\gamma^!}\Psi
=\mathrm{Div}_{\gamma^!}\Psi.$$
Since $\Psi(\pi)=\pi^!$, this gives
$\Psi(\upsilon)
=-\Psi\mathrm{Div}_{\gamma}(\pi)
=-\mathrm{Div}_{\gamma^!}(\pi^!)
=\upsilon^!.$


Let $M_x$ and $M_y$ denote the matrices of
$\overline\upsilon$ on
$\operatorname{span}_k\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}$ and
$\operatorname{span}_k\{y_1,\ldots,y_n\}$, respectively.
On the spaces of linear generators, the modular derivations of $A$ and $A^!$ have matrices
$$
\begin{pmatrix} M_x&0\\0&M_y\end{pmatrix}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\begin{pmatrix} M_x^{\mathsf T}&0\\0&-M_y^{\mathsf T}\end{pmatrix},
$$
respectively. These matrices are diagonalizable over $k$ simultaneously.

For either algebra, diagonalizability on the space of
linear generators is equivalent to diagonalizability
on the whole algebra. Indeed, a homogeneous eigenbasis
of generators yields a monomial eigenbasis by the
Leibniz rule. Conversely, the restriction of a
diagonalizable operator to an invariant subspace is
diagonalizable.
Hence the derivation of $A$ associated with $\upsilon$ is
diagonalizable if and only if the derivation of
$A^!$ associated with $\upsilon^!$ is.
head: environment

title: Remark
head: environment

title: Corollary
body_md:
Let $A=\mathcal{O}(k^{m||n})$ or
$\mathcal{O}(k^{n\wedge m})$, equipped with the corresponding
mixed volume form chosen above.
If $\pi$ is diagonal with respect to the specified
homogeneous linear coordinates, then its modular vector
field $\upsilon=-\mathrm{Div}_{\gamma}(\pi)$ is
diagonalizable over $k$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
For $A=\mathcal{O}(k^{m||n})$, the divergence of a diagonal
bivector is a linear combination of the coordinate Euler
vector fields. Thus the ordinary derivation corresponding
to $\upsilon$ acts diagonally on the monomial basis of $A$.
The dual case follows from
Proposition~\ref{modulardual} and the preservation of
diagonal Poisson structures under \eqref{corres}.
head: environment

label: comdiagram
title: Theorem
head: environment

label: correspondence
title: Proof
body_md:
Recall the polyvector and mixed form isomorphisms $\Psi$ and $\Phi$ from the proof of Proposition~\ref{modulardual}:
\begin{align}\label{correspondence}
\Psi:&\quad x_i\mapsto\partial_{\xi_i},\quad
 y_j\mapsto\partial_{\eta_j},\quad
 \partial_{x_i}\mapsto\xi_i,\quad\partial_{y_j}\mapsto\eta_j,\\
\Phi:&\quad x_i\mapsto\partial_{\xi_i},\quad
 y_j^*\mapsto d\eta_j,\quad dx_i\mapsto\xi_i^*,\quad
 \partial_{y_j}\mapsto\eta_j.\label{correspondence2}
\end{align}
They preserve degrees. The identities
$\Psi[\pi,P]=[\pi^!,\Psi(P)]$ and
$\Phi\tilde\iota_P=\tilde\iota_{\Psi(P)}\Phi$, together
with $\Phi\tilde d=\tilde d\Phi$ and
$\Psi(\upsilon)=\upsilon^!$, give
$$
\Psi\delta^\pi=\delta^{\pi^!}\Psi,\qquad
\Phi\partial_\upsilon=\partial_{\upsilon^!}\Phi.
$$
Thus $\Psi$ and $\Phi$ induce the left and right vertical
isomorphisms in \eqref{diagPoisson}, respectively.
The horizontal maps are induced by volume contraction,
as in Theorem~\ref{horiso}. Finally, the identity
$$
\Phi D_\gamma=D_{\gamma^!}\Psi,
$$
proved in Proposition~\ref{modulardual}, shows that the square commutes on representatives and hence on (co)homology. This argument applies without a diagonalizability hypothesis.
head: environment

label: isodiff
title: Theorem
body_md:
\label{isodiff}
Under the hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{comdiagram},
assume that the modular derivation of $A$ is
diagonalizable over $k$.
Then $(\Psi_*,\Phi_*)$ is an isomorphism between
the differential calculi with duality
$$
\bigl(
\mathrm{HP}^{\bullet,\bullet}(A),
\widetilde{\mathrm{HP}}_{\bullet,\bullet}(A;\upsilon),
\wedge,\tilde\iota,[-,-],\tilde d,[\gamma]
\bigr),
\bigl(
\mathrm{HP}^{\bullet,\bullet}(A^!),
\widetilde{\mathrm{HP}}_{\bullet,\bullet}
(A^!;\upsilon^!),
\wedge,\tilde\iota,[-,-],\tilde d,[\gamma^!]
\bigr).
$$
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{modulardual}, the modular
derivation of $A^!$ is also diagonalizable.
Corollary~\ref{diffcaldual} therefore supplies both
differential calculi with duality.

By \cite[Proposition~3.19]{CY}, the maps $\Psi$ and
$\Phi$ satisfy
$\Psi(P\wedge Q)=\Psi(P)\wedge\Psi(Q)$,
$\Psi[P,Q]=[\Psi(P),\Psi(Q)]$,
and
$\Phi\tilde\iota_P=\tilde\iota_{\Psi(P)}\Phi$,
$\Phi\tilde d=\tilde d\Phi$.
Theorem~\ref{comdiagram} shows that these maps
intertwine the Poisson differentials. Hence the
product, bracket and contraction identities descend
to (co)homology.

Moreover, $\Psi(\upsilon)=\upsilon^!$ gives
$\Phi L_\upsilon=L_{\upsilon^!}\Phi$.
Thus $\Phi$ preserves eigenspaces and intertwines the
zero-eigenvalue inclusions and projections.
Consequently,
$\Phi_*\tilde d=\tilde d\Phi_*$,
where $\tilde d$ on twisted Poisson homology denotes
the transported operator defined after
Theorem~\ref{diagonalizable}.

Finally, $\Phi(\gamma)=\gamma^!$, so $\Phi_*$
preserves the fundamental classes. This proves
compatibility with all the calculus operations
and with the duality.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By Proposition~\ref{modulardual}, the dual modular derivation is diagonalizable. Theorem~\ref{mainthm1.1} therefore gives BV structures on both Poisson cohomologies. By Theorems~\ref{comdiagram} and~\ref{isodiff}, the induced maps satisfy $\Phi_*\mathrm{PD}=\mathrm{PD}^!\Psi_*$ and $\Phi_*B=B^!\Phi_*$. Hence
$$
\Psi_*\Delta
=-\Psi_*\mathrm{PD}^{-1}B\mathrm{PD}
=-(\mathrm{PD}^!)^{-1}B^!\mathrm{PD}^!\Psi_*
=\Delta^!\Psi_*.
$$
The map $\Psi_*$ also preserves the product and bracket,
and hence is an isomorphism of BV algebras.
head: environment

label: ex:nonunimodular-22
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:nonunimodular-22}
Consider $A=\mathcal O(k^{2||2})$, with coordinates
$x_1,x_2,y_1,y_2$, and let
$$
\begin{aligned}
\pi=
x_1x_2\partial_{x_1}\wedge\partial_{x_2}
-y_1y_2\partial_{y_1}\wedge\partial_{y_2}
+\sum_{i,j=1}^{2}
x_i y_j\partial_{x_i}\wedge\partial_{y_j}.
\end{aligned}
$$
The bivector $\pi$ is diagonal and quadratic of degree $(0,-2)$. It is a linear combination of polyvector products of coordinate Euler derivations, which commute pairwise. Hence $[\pi,\pi]=0$.

For the mixed volume form
$\gamma=dx_1\wedge dx_2\wedge y_1^*\wedge y_2^*$,
direct mixed contraction gives
$$
\upsilon=-\mathrm{Div}_{\gamma}(\pi)
=-x_1\partial_{x_1}
-3x_2\partial_{x_2}
-3y_1\partial_{y_1}
-y_2\partial_{y_2}.
$$
In particular,
$\upsilon
(x_1^a x_2^b y_1^{\varepsilon_1}y_2^{\varepsilon_2})=
-(a+3b+3\varepsilon_1+\varepsilon_2)
x_1^a x_2^b y_1^{\varepsilon_1}y_2^{\varepsilon_2}$,
where $\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\in\{0,1\}$.
Thus the modular derivation is nonzero and diagonalizable. The structure $\pi$ is therefore non-unimodular, and Theorem~\ref{mainthm1.1} gives a BV structure on $\mathrm{HP}^{\bullet,\bullet}(A)$.

The coordinate Euler fields commute with $\pi$ and $\upsilon$.
Since
$\mathrm{Div}_\gamma(x_i\partial_{x_i})=1$ and
$\mathrm{Div}_\gamma(y_j\partial_{y_j})=-1$,
$\Delta[x_i\partial_{x_i}]=-[1]$,
$\Delta[y_j\partial_{y_j}]=[1]$.
Since the Euler fields commute, \eqref{eq:second-order} shows that $\Delta$ restricts to a graded derivation on the subalgebra generated by their classes.
In particular,
\begin{align*}
\Delta[x_1x_2\partial_{x_1}\wedge\partial_{x_2}]
&=[x_1\partial_{x_1}]-[x_2\partial_{x_2}],\\
\Delta[y_1y_2\partial_{y_1}\wedge\partial_{y_2}]
&=[y_1\partial_{y_1}]-[y_2\partial_{y_2}],\\
\Delta[x_i y_j\partial_{x_i}\wedge\partial_{y_j}]
&=-[x_i\partial_{x_i}]-[y_j\partial_{y_j}].
\end{align*}
To see that $[\upsilon]\ne0$, assign polynomial degree one
to each coordinate. Since $\pi$ has quadratic coefficients,
the coefficients of $[f,\pi]$ have no terms of degree less
than two for any $f\in A$. 
Thus $\upsilon$, a nonzero vector field with linear
coefficients, is not of the form $[f,\pi]$ for any $f\in A$.
Since the Poisson differential increases polyvector length
by one, this excludes all possible coboundaries for $\upsilon$.
By Remark~\ref{rem:modular-class-bv}, we therefore obtain
$\Delta[\pi]=[\upsilon]\ne0$.

On $A^!=\mathcal O(k^{2\wedge2})$, the dual Poisson bivector  is
$$
\pi^!=\xi_1\xi_2\partial_{\xi_1}\wedge\partial_{\xi_2}
-\eta_1\eta_2\partial_{\eta_1}\wedge\partial_{\eta_2}
-\sum_{i,j=1}^{2}\xi_i\eta_j
\partial_{\xi_i}\wedge\partial_{\eta_j}.
$$
For $\gamma^!=\xi_1^*\wedge\xi_2^*\wedge d\eta_1\wedge d\eta_2$,
$\upsilon^!=-\xi_1\partial_{\xi_1}-3\xi_2\partial_{\xi_2}
+3\eta_1\partial_{\eta_1}+\eta_2\partial_{\eta_2}$.
The dual modular derivation is again nonzero and diagonalizable.
Under the correspondence
$x_i\partial_{x_i}\mapsto\xi_i\partial_{\xi_i}$,
$y_j\partial_{y_j}\mapsto-\eta_j\partial_{\eta_j}$,
Theorem~\ref{mainthm} identifies the BV operators.
head: environment
name: A non-unimodular structure on $k^{2||2}$

label: ex:nonunimodular-13
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:nonunimodular-13}
Consider $A=\mathcal O(k^{1||3})$, with coordinates
$x,y_1,y_2,y_3$ of degrees
$|x|=(0,0)$ and $|y_j|=(1,0)$.
Let
$$
\pi=
\sum_{j=1}^{3}xy_j\partial_x\wedge\partial_{y_j}
-\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq3}
y_i y_j\partial_{y_i}\wedge\partial_{y_j}.
$$
As in the preceding example, this is a diagonal quadratic
Poisson structure of degree $(0,-2)$.

For
$\gamma=dx\wedge y_1^*\wedge y_2^*\wedge y_3^*$,
the modular vector field is
$$
\upsilon=-\mathrm{Div}_{\gamma}(\pi)
=-3x\partial_x
-3y_1\partial_{y_1}
-y_2\partial_{y_2}
+y_3\partial_{y_3}.
$$
Its action on monomials is
$\upsilon
(x^a y_1^{\varepsilon_1}
y_2^{\varepsilon_2}y_3^{\varepsilon_3})
=
(-3a-3\varepsilon_1-\varepsilon_2+\varepsilon_3)
x^a y_1^{\varepsilon_1}
y_2^{\varepsilon_2}y_3^{\varepsilon_3},$
where $\varepsilon_j\in\{0,1\}$.
Hence the modular derivation is diagonalizable. Since $\upsilon\ne0$, Proposition~\ref{prop:canonical-volume} excludes a mixed volume form that is a Poisson cycle, so $\pi$ is non-unimodular.
Its modular class is nonzero by the polynomial degree
argument in Example~\ref{ex:nonunimodular-22}.
Thus Theorem~\ref{mainthm1.1} applies here as well.

On the subalgebra generated by the coordinate Euler classes,
$\Delta$ is the graded derivation determined by
$\Delta[x\partial_x]=-[1]$,
$\Delta[y_j\partial_{y_j}]=[1]$ for $j=1,2,3$.
Consequently,
\begin{align*}
\Delta[xy_j\partial_x\wedge\partial_{y_j}]
=-[x\partial_x]-[y_j\partial_{y_j}],\quad
\Delta[y_i y_j\partial_{y_i}\wedge\partial_{y_j}]
=[y_i\partial_{y_i}]-[y_j\partial_{y_j}]
\quad(i<j).
\end{align*}
Thus
$\Delta[\pi]=-3[x\partial_x]-3[y_1\partial_{y_1}]
-[y_2\partial_{y_2}]+[y_3\partial_{y_3}]
=[\upsilon]\ne0$.

On $A^!=\mathcal O(k^{3\wedge1})$, the dual structure is
$$
\pi^!=-\sum_{j=1}^{3}\xi\eta_j
\partial_\xi\wedge\partial_{\eta_j}
-\sum_{1\leq i<j\leq3}\eta_i\eta_j
\partial_{\eta_i}\wedge\partial_{\eta_j}.
$$
For $\gamma^!=\xi^*\wedge d\eta_1\wedge d\eta_2\wedge d\eta_3$,
$\upsilon^!=-3\xi\partial_\xi
+3\eta_1\partial_{\eta_1}
+\eta_2\partial_{\eta_2}-\eta_3\partial_{\eta_3}$.
The resulting modular derivation of $A^!$ is nonzero and diagonalizable.
The correspondence
$x\partial_x\mapsto\xi\partial_\xi$,
$y_j\partial_{y_j}\mapsto-\eta_j\partial_{\eta_j}$
identifies the BV operators by Theorem~\ref{mainthm}.
head: environment
name: A non-unimodular structure on $k^{1||3}$

label: ex:nondiagonal
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:nondiagonal}
On $k^{3||0}$, consider the Poisson structure
$$
\pi=x_1^2\partial_{x_2}\wedge\partial_{x_3}
+x_1x_2\partial_{x_1}\wedge\partial_{x_2}
-x_1x_3\partial_{x_1}\wedge\partial_{x_3}.
$$
For the standard volume,
$$
\upsilon=-x_2\partial_{x_2}+x_3\partial_{x_3},\qquad
\upsilon(x_1^a x_2^b x_3^c)=(c-b)x_1^a x_2^b x_3^c.
$$
Hence the modular derivation is diagonalizable and nonzero.
The zero locus of $\pi$ is the hyperplane $x_1=0$.
In contrast, a diagonal bivector vanishes on every
coordinate axis, so its zero locus spans the whole
ambient space. The dimension of the linear span of the zero locus is invariant under invertible linear coordinate changes. Hence $\pi$ cannot be diagonal in any linear coordinates.
Theorem~\ref{mainthm} applies to this non-unimodular
structure and its Koszul dual.
head: environment
name: A non-diagonal structure

label: ex:nilpotent-modular
title: Example
body_md:
\label{ex:nilpotent-modular}
On $k^{2||0}$, let $\pi=x_1^2\partial_{x_1}\wedge\partial_{x_2}$.
It is Poisson because the space has dimension two.
For $\gamma=dx_1\wedge dx_2$, our contraction order gives
$D_\gamma(\pi)=-x_1^2$ and $\upsilon=-2x_1\partial_{x_2}$.
On $\operatorname{span}\{x_1,x_2\}$, the modular derivation is a nonzero nilpotent operator. Hence the modular derivation is not diagonalizable. Proposition~\ref{modulardual} implies the same conclusion for the dual modular derivation.
head: environment
name: Failure of diagonalizability

label: rem:homogeneous-scope
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:homogeneous-scope}
On $\mathcal O(k^{m||n})$, suppose that the coefficients
of $\pi$ are homogeneous of polynomial degree $d$.
Then its modular derivation shifts polynomial degree by
$d-2$. If $d>2$, the lowest nonzero homogeneous term of
an eigenvector rules out a nonzero eigenvalue; if $d<2$,
the highest nonzero term does so. Thus, when $d\ne2$,
all eigenvalues are zero, and diagonalizability forces
$\upsilon=0$. 
Among Poisson structures homogeneous in polynomial degree, the non-unimodular case of Theorem~\ref{mainthm1.1} is therefore quadratic. The theorem also applies to inhomogeneous Poisson structures of degree $(0,-2)$.
